planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Picturata scorches badly in direct sun and needs deeper shade than most variegated shrubs.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, avoiding direct sun, which scorches and bleaches the distinctive foliage. Picturata is an eye-catching aucuba cultivar with an unusual variegation pattern reversed from the more common gold-dust type: each glossy, leathery leaf has a bold splash of gold-yellow in the center surrounded by a dark green margin, rather than gold speckles scattered over green. Like other aucubas, it is one of the few broadleaf evergreen shrubs that thrives in deep, dry shade under trees where little else stays attractive, making it valuable for difficult shaded foundation plantings and understory beds. Female plants produce bright red berries in winter if a male aucuba is nearby for pollination; little pruning is needed beyond removing damaged or leggy stems in spring.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Aurea tolerates a wider range of light than most nandina and holds its yellow-green color in shade better than red-toned cultivars hold their color.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Aurea is tolerant of a wide range of soils and light levels once established. Unlike the many red-and-burgundy-toned nandina cultivars grown for winter foliage color, Aurea keeps its lance-shaped leaflets a soft yellow-green year-round, with creamy-white summer flower clusters followed by unusual pale yellow berries instead of the typical bright red, giving it a distinctly different look for gardeners wanting variety among their heavenly bamboo plantings. Its upright, cane-like growth habit is identical to other nandina cultivars, spreading slowly by underground rhizomes to form a loose colony over time. Prune by removing the oldest canes at ground level each year to keep the planting full from top to bottom rather than shearing, which leaves bare lower stems.

common_name: Flirt Nandina (Dwarf Compact Red-Tipped Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; new growth color is most vivid with several hours of direct sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 18–24 inches apart for a low mass planting or border edge. Flirt is a dwarf, mounding nandina bred to stay compact without the tall, leggy cane growth of larger nandina cultivars, producing new foliage that emerges bright red and matures to green through summer before returning to deep red-burgundy in fall and winter cold. Its small size and dense, tidy habit fit foundation plantings, mixed containers, and border edges where full-size nandina would need constant cutting back, and it is sterile, producing no berries and therefore no risk of the self-seeding that has made standard nandina invasive in parts of the Southeast. Little pruning is needed beyond removing occasional damaged stems.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Compactum holds its lower, denser form best out of hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade, and avoid the hottest afternoon sun, which can scorch the glossy, holly-like leaflets. Compactum is a dwarf selection of the Pacific Northwest native Oregon grape, staying under 3 feet tall and wide — roughly half the size of the species — while still producing the same fragrant, bright yellow spring flower clusters followed by dusty-blue, edible (if tart) berries beloved by songbirds, and the same spiny, holly-like evergreen foliage that turns purple-bronze in winter cold. Its smaller stature suits it to foundation plantings and shaded borders where full-size Oregon grape would eventually crowd the space. Prune only lightly, if at all, since its naturally compact habit needs little maintenance to stay tidy.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wheeler's Dwarf tolerates salt spray and coastal conditions well, making it a common choice near the Gulf.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wheeler's Dwarf tolerates coastal salt spray, wind, and poor soil better than many broadleaf evergreens, making it a reliable low hedge or foundation plant in Gulf Coast landscapes. This dwarf pittosporum forms a dense, mounding shrub of small, glossy, leathery, deep-green leaves rarely reaching more than 2 feet tall, with clusters of small, cream-white flowers in spring that carry a strong orange-blossom fragrance detectable from several feet away, the trait that gives the species its common name of mock orange. Its naturally low, tidy habit needs little shearing to maintain shape, and it holds up well to both heat and the Gulf Coast's high humidity. Prune, if needed, right after the spring bloom to preserve next year's flowers.

common_name: Cinnamon Girl Distylium (Bronze New-Growth Evergreen Shade Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to full shade; distylium is exceptionally adaptable to both light levels and soil moisture once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to full shade — distylium is one of the most adaptable evergreen shrubs available, thriving in nearly any light level and tolerating both drought and occasional wet soil once established. Cinnamon Girl produces new growth flushed a warm coppery bronze-red before maturing to lustrous dark green, giving season-long color contrast on a dense, mounding, wider-than-tall shrub that functions as a low-maintenance, deer-resistant alternative to boxwood or Indian hawthorn. Small, inconspicuous red flowers appear in late winter but are not the plant's main ornamental feature. It requires little pruning to hold its naturally tidy, rounded form, and tolerates heat, humidity, and both sun and shade with equal ease, making it a versatile foundation or mass-planting shrub across a wide range of garden conditions.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; So Sweet is a mid-size hosta with narrow, pointed, deep-green leaves edged in a creamy-white margin, forming a neat, symmetrical mound that works well as an accent or in mass plantings under trees. In midsummer it sends up tall scapes of pale lavender flowers with an unusually strong, sweet fragrance detectable from several feet away, a trait shared by relatively few hosta cultivars and one that adds a second season of interest beyond the foliage. Divide congested clumps in early spring or fall every 4–5 years to maintain vigor, and watch for slugs, which can disfigure the leaves in consistently damp conditions.
